## What it is

This entry is about *writing*. Standard advice says to cut every unnecessary word. Gelman observes that "unnecessary" words often do real work. They set the rhythm, signal transitions and give the reader time to absorb a point. Strip all the padding from the seats and the ride gets bumpy. Prose that is too compressed is hard to read even when every word carries meaning.

## Why it matters

Statistical writing is especially prone to over-compression: dense sentences, stacked qualifiers, results crammed into one paragraph. Readers then misread or skim. A little redundancy, such as restating the main finding, a signpost sentence or a concrete example, makes technical writing easier to follow. The aim is not the fewest words. It is the most understanding per minute of reading.

## How it works

The simulation is an **analogy**: the tradeoff between rhythm and meaning looks a lot like the tradeoff between smoothness and fidelity in signal processing. Treat a text's "information" as a signal and the reader's experience as a moving average over it.

- **No padding** (window size 1): every bump of the raw signal comes through, and the ride is jarring.
- **Too much padding** (a huge window): the ride is smooth but the meaning, the actual shape of the signal, is lost.
- **The right amount:** the shape survives and the noise is absorbed.

This is a toy picture of the writing advice, not a model of prose.

## Simulated example

A smooth underlying "message" is observed with noise. Vary the amount of padding, meaning the smoothing window, and watch the error between what the reader experiences and the true message.

```{ojs}
import {rng, range, mean, fmt} from "../js/stats.js"
```

```{ojs}
viewof padding = Inputs.range([1, 61], {value: 1, step: 2, label: "Padding (smoothing window)"})
viewof seed = Inputs.range([1, 500], {value: 28, step: 1, label: "Random seed"})
```

```{ojs}
ride = {
  const r = rng(seed);
  const n = 200;
  const msg = range(n).map(i => Math.sin(i / 18) + 0.5 * Math.sin(i / 7));
  const obs = msg.map(v => v + r.normal(0, 0.6));
  const smooth = w => obs.map((_, i) => {
    const lo = Math.max(0, i - (w - 1) / 2), hi = Math.min(n - 1, i + (w - 1) / 2);
    return mean(obs.slice(lo, hi + 1));
  });
  const err = w => Math.sqrt(mean(smooth(w).map((v, i) => (v - msg[i]) ** 2)));
  const curve = range(31).map(k => 2 * k + 1).map(w => ({w, err: err(w)}));
  return {series: smooth(padding).map((v, i) => ({i, reader: v, msg: msg[i], raw: obs[i]})), curve};
}
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  height: 240,
  x: {label: "Position in text"},
  y: {label: "Signal", grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.dot(ride.series, {x: "i", y: "raw", r: 1, fill: "#bbb"}),
    Plot.line(ride.series, {x: "i", y: "msg", stroke: "currentColor", strokeDasharray: "4 3"}),
    Plot.line(ride.series, {x: "i", y: "reader", stroke: "#2166ac", strokeWidth: 2})
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  height: 180,
  x: {label: "Padding (window size)"},
  y: {label: "Error vs true message", grid: true},
  marks: [Plot.line(ride.curve, {x: "w", y: "err", stroke: "#2166ac"}), Plot.dot(ride.curve.filter(d => d.w === padding), {x: "w", y: "err", r: 6, fill: "#d6604d"})]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const best = ride.curve.reduce((a, b) => a.err < b.err ? a : b);
  return html`<div class="sim-readout">${md`At padding ${padding}, the error is **${fmt(ride.curve.find(d => d.w === padding).err, 3)}**. The best ride is at a window of about **${best.w}** (error ${fmt(best.err, 3)}): some padding helps, and too much loses the message. As the analogy says: don't strip prose of every word that doesn't carry new information.`}</div>`;
}
```

## Key takeaways

::: takeaways
- "Omit needless words" can be overdone. Rhythm and redundancy help readers.
- In technical writing, signposts, restatements and examples are padding that makes the ride smoother.
- The goal is understanding per minute of reading, not the fewest words.
:::
